summary: Suggests a straightforward convention for defining traps, the alerts that devices send unprompted, for use with SNMP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1215 describes a way to write down SNMP trap definitions in a MIB. It also warns that traps are strongly discouraged in the Internet-standard network management framework.

subtitle: A convention for recording SNMP trap definitions in management information modules.

tldr.problem: The Internet-standard Structure of Management Information did not provide a convenient notation for defining traps used by experimental MIBs.
tldr.mechanism: The memo suggests a TRAP-TYPE macro with an enterprise identifier and optional variables, description, and reference, then maps these fields to an SNMP Trap-PDU.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo defines no standard and strongly discourages creating new traps. It presents a convention for concise descriptions, including existing traps.

today: RFC 1215 is an Informational memo published in March 1991. It does not specify a standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Background to SNMP Management Information
sections.content:
The memo reviews how the Internet's network management work developed around the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), the Structure of Management Information (SMI), and the Management Information Base (MIB). The initial plan aimed to support both SNMP and the OSI management framework.

The memo says those frameworks had different requirements, so the compatibility requirement was suspended. The Internet-standard management documents then described how managed objects are defined, which objects are in the MIB, and how SNMP manages them.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP uses a set of rules for describing managed objects and a list of those objects. RFC 1215 explains why that set of rules needed a trap-definition convention.

sections.title: Why the Memo Suggests a Trap Macro
sections.content:
The SMI was intended to be independent of a specific protocol and did not define a way to write traps. SNMP already had standardized traps and allowed enterprises to send enterprise-specific traps, but experimental MIBs also needed a concise notation.

The memo says use of traps in the Internet-standard network management framework is strongly discouraged. It presents TRAP-TYPE to describe existing traps concisely, not to encourage new traps.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo provides a notation for documenting traps used by experimental MIBs. It cautions readers not to treat the notation as encouragement to create new traps.

sections.title: The TRAP-TYPE Definition
sections.content:
A TRAP-TYPE definition requires an ENTERPRISE clause containing an object identifier. It may also include a VARIABLES list, a DESCRIPTION, and a REFERENCE. The macro's value is an integer assigned to the trap by the registration authority for that enterprise.

The macro expands conceptually during implementation, not at run time. The DESCRIPTION clause must be present if the MIB module does not describe the trap elsewhere. A REFERENCE can point to a related trap, event, or alarm in another MIB module.
sections.plainLanguage: A trap definition names the enterprise and gives the trap a number. Optional clauses list data carried with the trap and explain its meaning.

sections.title: How the Clauses Map to an SNMP Trap
sections.content:
The ENTERPRISE value goes into the enterprise field of the SNMP Trap-PDU. Objects in VARIABLES go, in order, into its variable-bindings field; an agent may add more variables after them. For an enterprise-specific trap, the macro's integer goes in specific-trap and generic-trap is set to enterpriseSpecific(6).

There is a special convention when ENTERPRISE is snmp, identified in the memo as { mib-2 11 }. In that case, sysObjectID supplies the enterprise field, the macro value supplies generic-trap, and specific-trap is zero. The serialized message must not exceed 484 octets when variables are added for these standard traps.
sections.plainLanguage: Each clause supplies a value for a field in the SNMP trap message. A special mapping lets the same macro describe the existing standard traps.

sections.title: Enterprise and Standard Trap Examples
sections.content:
The enterprise-specific example defines myLinkDown under enterprise identifier 9999. It includes ifIndex, uses value 2, and describes a communications-link failure recognized by the agent.

The memo also shows definitions for coldStart, warmStart, linkDown, linkUp, authenticationFailure, and egpNeighborLoss, with values 0 through 5. For authenticationFailure, implementations must be able to generate the trap and must also be able to suppress it through an implementation-specific mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show one enterprise-defined link-failure trap and definitions for six existing standard traps. The macro records their names, values, and meanings.

viz.caption: THE SIX STANDARD TRAPS SHOWN IN RFC 1215

items.label: coldStart
items.desc: The sender is reinitializing and its configuration or implementation may change.

items.label: warmStart
items.desc: The sender is reinitializing without changing configuration or implementation.

items.label: linkDown
items.desc: The sender recognized a communications-link failure.

items.label: linkUp
items.desc: The sender recognized that a communications link came up.

items.label: authenticationFailure
items.desc: The sender received a message that was not properly authenticated.

items.label: egpNeighborLoss
items.desc: An EGP neighbor was marked down.
